subject: SCI
overview: This course follows the CA NGSS for grade 5: matter, plants and energy, ecosystems, Earth's systems, and space. Each week is hands-on — gather materials ahead, let your child predict before testing, and record everything in a science notebook. Use claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) writing to check understanding. Supervise heat, chemicals and outdoor night observations.

weeks.prep: Sugar, clear cups, warm water, kitchen scale (grams), spoons, a dark plate, and a science notebook. Test the scale first; tare it with the empty cup.
misconceptions: Thinking dissolved sugar is gone or 'melted.' Dissolving means sugar particles spread out among water particles; it is still there (you can taste it).
Thinking dissolved things weigh nothing. The mixture weighs the water plus the sugar.
Confusing dissolving with melting. Melting needs heat and changes one substance from solid to liquid.

days.guide: Stir a spoonful of sugar into warm water until you can't see it. Your child tastes a drop and writes observations and at least two questions in the notebook. Ask: 'If you can't see it, how do you know it's there?'

questions.q: The sugar 'disappeared.' Is it still in the water? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes — the water tastes sweet, so sugar particles are spread throughout the water, too small to see.

days.guide: Weigh the water, weigh the sugar, then mix and weigh again. Record in a table and compare the mixture's weight with the sum.

questions.q: Water 200 g and sugar 20 g are mixed. Predict the weight of the sugar water.
questions.a: 220 g — mass is conserved when sugar dissolves.

days.guide: Place a few drops of sugar water on a dark plate in a sunny window. Your child writes a prediction of what will remain after the water evaporates and why.

questions.q: What do you predict will be left on the plate?
questions.a: Sugar crystals — only the water evaporates; the sugar particles stay behind.

days.guide: Check the plate with a magnifier for crystals. Your child draws a before-and-after particle model: sugar particles clumped in a crystal, then spread among water particles.

questions.q: What does the crystal residue tell us?
questions.a: The sugar was in the water the whole time; when water particles evaporated, sugar particles came back together as crystals.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER paragraph answering 'Is the sugar still there?' using the weight data and evaporation evidence. Review it with the rubric.

questions.q: Give a model claim and the two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: Claim: The sugar is still in the water as particles too small to see. Evidence: the mixture weighed the same as the water plus the sugar, and sugar crystals were left after evaporation.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = clear, accurate claim; specific evidence with numbers from the data; reasoning that links evidence to the science idea (particles, conservation, etc.); 3 = accurate claim and evidence, reasoning partial; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or inaccurate. Particle model: before = sugar particles packed together in a crystal, water separate; after = sugar particles evenly spread among water particles; labels and a key.

weeks.prep: Balloons, a ruler or dowel, string, a needle-free syringe, a plastic bottle, a ball and pump, kitchen scale, a cup, a paper towel and a bowl of water. Bookmark PhET 'States of Matter: Basics' (free online).
misconceptions: Thinking air is 'nothing.' Air is matter: it takes up space and has weight.
Believing a pumped-up ball weighs the same. Extra air particles add a small amount of weight.
Thinking particles in a gas get smaller when compressed. The particles stay the same size; the spaces between them shrink.

days.guide: Stuff a dry paper towel in the bottom of a cup, flip it upside down and push it straight down into the bowl of water. Lift it out and check the towel. Your child explains why it stayed dry.

questions.q: Why does the paper towel stay dry?
questions.a: Air trapped in the cup takes up space and keeps the water from coming in.

days.guide: Hang two equal inflated balloons from each end of a ruler balanced on a string. Pop one balloon (carefully, safety glasses or at arm's length) and observe the tip. Record findings.

questions.q: Which way does the balance tip after one balloon is popped, and why?
questions.a: It tips toward the full balloon, because the air inside it has weight (the popped balloon lost its compressed air).

days.guide: Weigh a deflated ball, pump it up and weigh again. Then cap a syringe with your finger and push the plunger. Your child describes what happens to the particles.

questions.q: Why does the pumped ball weigh more?
questions.a: More air particles were added, and air has weight.

questions.q: What happens to air particles when you push the syringe?
questions.a: They are pushed closer together (compressed), but they are not destroyed.

days.guide: Explore the PhET simulation with your child, switching between solid, liquid and gas. Your child sketches particle arrangements and describes motion for each.

questions.q: How do particles move in a solid, liquid and gas?
questions.a: Solid: vibrate in place, tightly packed; liquid: close together but slide past each other; gas: far apart and moving fast in all directions.

days.guide: Your child revises the week 1 particle model to include gases and writes how particles too small to see can still have weight. Lay the two models side by side and ask what needs to change. Check that gas particles are drawn far apart with motion arrows and that the written explanation cites the balloon or ball evidence.

questions.q: How can particles too small to see have weight?
questions.a: Each particle has a tiny mass; billions together add up to a weight we can measure, like the air in a ball.

weeks.assessment_key: Revised model: shows gas particles far apart and moving, labels solid/liquid/gas, explains that each particle has mass. Data tables: ball weight before < after; balance tipped toward full balloon; towel dry. Proficient explanation uses evidence from at least two investigations.

weeks.prep: Collect samples: aluminum foil, steel paper clip, plastic spoon, wooden stick, rubber band, glass marble, salt, baking soda; a magnet, flashlight, simple circuit kit (battery, bulb, wires), metal/plastic/wooden spoons and hot water (adult handles). Pre-test the circuit.
misconceptions: Thinking all metals are magnetic. Only some (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are; aluminum foil is not.
Thinking 'heavy' is a property used to identify a material regardless of size. Use properties like hardness, conductivity and magnetism.
Thinking metal spoons feel colder because they are colder. They conduct heat away from your hand faster.

days.guide: Your child observes each sample and records color, texture, hardness (does it scratch with a nail?) and flexibility in a table.

questions.q: Which is harder: the glass marble or the wooden stick? How can you test it?
questions.a: The glass marble; a scratch test with a nail scratches wood but not glass.

days.guide: Test each sample with a magnet and with a flashlight beam (shiny/reflective or not). Add results to the table.

questions.q: Which samples did the magnet attract?
questions.a: Only the steel paper clip; aluminum foil, plastic, wood, rubber, glass, salt and baking soda are not magnetic.

questions.q: Which reflect light best?
questions.a: Aluminum foil (shiny metal) and the glass marble.

days.guide: Build a circuit with a gap; place each sample in the gap. If the bulb lights, it is a conductor. Record results.

questions.q: Which samples completed the circuit?
questions.a: Aluminum foil and the paper clip (metals); plastic, wood, rubber, glass and dry salt are insulators.

days.guide: Stand metal, plastic and wooden spoons in hot water (adult pours). After 3 minutes your child carefully touches each handle and ranks warmth.

questions.q: Which handle warms fastest and why?
questions.a: The metal spoon, because metal is a good thermal conductor; plastic and wood are insulators.

days.guide: Give your child 3 'mystery' samples. They use the property table to identify each and explain which properties gave it away.

questions.q: A shiny, bendable material conducts electricity but isn't attracted by a magnet. What could it be?
questions.a: Aluminum foil.

weeks.assessment_key: Property table complete for 8 samples across 7 properties. Mystery identification: correct material plus 2 supporting properties each (e.g., paper clip = magnetic + conducts; plastic spoon = insulator + not magnetic + flexible; glass marble = hard, transparent, insulator).

weeks.prep: Baking soda, salt, sugar, cornstarch, flour, vinegar, red cabbage juice (boil chopped red cabbage in water, strain) or iodine (adult only — poisonous, stains), magnifier, muffin tin, labels. Safety: no tasting powders in this lab.
misconceptions: Identifying a powder by look alone. Several white powders look alike; use multiple tests.
Thinking fizzing means boiling. Fizzing is a gas (carbon dioxide) being produced by a reaction.
Mixing up dissolving and settling. Dissolved powders disappear; undissolved ones settle or cloud the water.

days.guide: Your child examines each powder with a magnifier and records texture, crystal shape and feel (rubbed between fingers, then washed). Model the first powder by thinking aloud ('tiny cubes, gritty'). Remind your child to wash hands after touching and never taste.

questions.q: How do salt and sugar look under a magnifier?
questions.a: Salt crystals look like small cubes; sugar crystals are larger and more irregular, glassy grains.

questions.q: Which powders feel smooth and squeaky?
questions.a: Cornstarch (very fine and silky); flour is soft too.

days.guide: Add a spoonful of each powder to water and stir. Record dissolves, clumps or settles.

questions.q: Which powders dissolve?
questions.a: Salt and sugar dissolve; baking soda mostly dissolves; cornstarch and flour make cloudy water and settle.

days.guide: Test each powder with vinegar and with the indicator. Record fizzing and color change.

questions.q: Which powder fizzes with vinegar?
questions.a: Baking soda — it reacts to make carbon dioxide gas.

questions.q: What does iodine do with cornstarch and flour?
questions.a: Turns them blue-black because they contain starch. (With cabbage juice, baking soda turns it green-blue because it is a base.)

days.guide: Prepare a mystery powder (or a mix of two, e.g., baking soda + cornstarch). Your child runs the tests and compares with the chart.

questions.q: A mystery powder fizzes with vinegar and turns iodine blue-black. What is it?
questions.a: A mixture of baking soda and a starch (cornstarch or flour).

days.guide: Your child writes a CER identifying the mystery powder and takes a properties quiz. Have your child state the claim aloud first, then point to the rows of the chart that are the evidence. Score the CER with the rubric before the quiz.

questions.q: Why use several tests instead of one?
questions.a: Different powders share some properties; combining test results narrows it down to one identity.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = clear, accurate claim; specific evidence with numbers from the data; reasoning that links evidence to the science idea (particles, conservation, etc.); 3 = accurate claim and evidence, reasoning partial; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or inaccurate. Quiz key (suggested): 1) baking soda fizzes with vinegar 2) cornstarch/flour turn iodine blue-black 3) salt and sugar dissolve in water 4) cornstarch does not dissolve 5) baking soda turns cabbage juice green/blue (base) 6) properties are characteristics used to identify a substance.

weeks.prep: Ice cubes, zip bags, a pot with a lid (adult handles the stove), food coloring, cups of hot and cold tap water, a timer, poster paper. Write the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Thinking particles themselves melt or expand. The particles stay the same; their motion and spacing change.
Thinking the water on a cold lid leaked through. It is water vapor condensing.
Thinking steam you see is a gas. Visible 'steam' is tiny liquid droplets; water vapor is invisible.

days.guide: Place identical ice cubes in bags in different spots (hand, counter, sunny window). Time each until fully melted and graph the times.

questions.q: Why does ice melt fastest in your hand?
questions.a: Your hand transfers heat energy to the ice, making its particles move faster and break out of their fixed positions.

days.guide: Drop food coloring into hot and cold water at the same time. Your child observes and links speed to particle motion.

questions.q: Why does color spread faster in hot water?
questions.a: Hot water particles move faster and bump the color particles around more quickly.

days.guide: Adult boils water and holds a cold lid above it. Your child draws particle diagrams for evaporation (liquid to gas) and condensation (gas to liquid).

questions.q: Where do the drops on the lid come from?
questions.a: Water vapor from the boiling water cools on the lid and condenses into liquid.

days.guide: Your child creates a poster showing particles in solid, liquid and gas with labeled arrows for melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing. Sketch one state together, then your child completes the rest. Check spacing: solid packed in rows, liquid close but jumbled, gas far apart.

questions.q: Name the change from gas to liquid and from liquid to solid.
questions.a: Condensation; freezing.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test and have your child present the poster, explaining each arrow. Give the test without help. During the poster talk, ask 'What happens to the particles during condensation?' to check reasoning.

questions.q: Does a substance's mass change when it melts?
questions.a: No — the same particles are there, just arranged differently.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (suggested): 1) matter is made of particles too small to see 2) dissolved sugar is still present 3) air has weight and takes up space 4) gas particles are far apart and move quickly 5) metals conduct heat and electricity 6) baking soda fizzes in vinegar 7) melting = solid to liquid 8) evaporation = liquid to gas 9) condensation = gas to liquid 10) hot water spreads dye faster because particles move faster. Poster rubric: correct particle spacing for each state, four labeled changes, neat key.

weeks.prep: Kitchen scale (grams), ice cubes, sealed zip bags (double-bag), chocolate chips, warm-water bowl, graph paper. Wipe bags dry before every weighing.
misconceptions: Thinking melted water weighs less because it 'shrinks.' Mass stays the same; ice actually takes up more space than the same water.
Counting condensation on the outside of the bag. Dry the bag first or the scale shows extra water.
Treating a 1 g difference as proof. Small differences are measurement error.

days.guide: Ask: Will a sealed bag of ice weigh more, less or the same after melting? Your child writes a prediction and reason.

questions.q: Predict the weight of a sealed bag of ice after it melts.
questions.a: The same — no particles enter or leave the sealed bag.

days.guide: Weigh 3 sealed bags of ice, let them melt, dry the outsides, and reweigh. Record in a table.

questions.q: A bag of ice weighs 152 g; after melting it weighs 152 g. What does this show?
questions.a: Mass is conserved during melting.

days.guide: Weigh bags of water and freeze overnight. Also melt chocolate chips in a sealed bag in warm water and reweigh.

questions.q: Does freezing change weight?
questions.a: No — the water freezes but the weight stays the same.

days.guide: Your child makes a bar graph comparing before and after weights for all trials and calculates differences. Help set a y-axis scale that starts at a sensible number so small differences are visible. Ask: 'Are any differences bigger than 1–2 g? What could cause them?'

questions.q: If one trial shows a 1 g difference, what could explain it?
questions.a: Measurement error: a water drop on the outside, scale precision, or a tiny leak.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on whether weight is conserved, explaining small errors. Prompt: 'What evidence from your table supports your claim?' The reasoning should say the same particles stayed sealed in the bag.

questions.q: Write the claim.
questions.a: Weight is conserved during melting and freezing.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = clear, accurate claim; specific evidence with numbers from the data; reasoning that links evidence to the science idea (particles, conservation, etc.); 3 = accurate claim and evidence, reasoning partial; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or inaccurate. Bar graph: paired bars before/after for each trial, labeled axes in grams, title. Proficient CER explains that the same particles remain in the sealed bag.

weeks.prep: Sand, salt, paper clips, rice, coffee filter, sieve, magnet, water, kitchen scale, cups, trail mix ingredients.
misconceptions: Thinking a solution is not a mixture. A solution is a mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another.
Thinking salt is destroyed when dissolved. It can be recovered by evaporation.
Expecting to recover exactly 100% of the salt. Some sticks to the filter and cups.

days.guide: Make trail mix and a sand-salt mix. Weigh each part and the whole and check that weights add up.

questions.q: 20 g of sand + 15 g of salt = ? g of mixture.

days.guide: Your child plans a separation of sand, salt, paper clips and rice using properties: magnetism, particle size, and solubility. Ask questions rather than giving the order: 'What property does only the paper clip have? What can water do to salt but not sand?' Your child writes numbered steps.

questions.q: Give the order of steps.
questions.a: Magnet removes paper clips; sieve removes rice; add water to dissolve the salt; filter out the sand; evaporate the water to recover salt.

days.guide: Carry out the plan. Pour the salt water through the coffee filter and set it to evaporate on a plate.

questions.q: Why does the sand stay in the filter but the salt doesn't?
questions.a: Sand doesn't dissolve and its grains are too large; dissolved salt particles pass through with the water.

days.guide: Weigh the recovered salt and compare with the starting amount. Discuss differences.

questions.q: Why might you recover less salt than you started with?
questions.a: Some salt stays in the filter, sand or cups, or water hadn't fully evaporated.

days.guide: Your child writes a procedure for separating a new mixture (e.g., iron filings, sugar and pebbles) and takes a mixtures quiz. Read the procedure as if you were following it literally; if a step is unclear, your child revises it. Then give the quiz.

questions.q: Mixture or solution: salt water? sand and water?
questions.a: Salt water is a solution; sand and water is a mixture that is not a solution.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) mixture = substances combined but not chemically changed 2) solution = one substance dissolved evenly in another 3) magnet separates iron/steel 4) sieve separates by size 5) filtering separates undissolved solids 6) evaporation recovers dissolved solids. Procedure rubric: numbered steps, uses properties, materials listed.

weeks.prep: Baking soda, vinegar, milk, lemon juice, steel wool (wear gloves), 3 jars, balloons, red cabbage juice, 6 household liquids (lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda water, soap water, milk). Do not mix bleach or ammonia.
misconceptions: Thinking any change is a chemical reaction. Melting, dissolving and tearing are not; new substances must form.
Thinking bubbles always mean a reaction. Boiling water bubbles but makes no new substance.
Thinking rust is dirt on the metal. Rust is a new substance (iron oxide) formed from iron, oxygen and water.

days.guide: Teach the four signs: gas, color change, temperature change, new solid. Mix baking soda and vinegar in a cup; your child records observations.

questions.q: What sign of a chemical reaction do you see with baking soda and vinegar?
questions.a: Bubbles of a new gas (carbon dioxide); the cup also feels slightly cooler.

days.guide: Add lemon juice to warm milk and stir; compare with milk mixed with water. Adult warms the milk (not boiling). Your child records what they see in both cups and names which sign of a new substance appeared.

questions.q: What forms and is it a new substance?
questions.a: Solid curds form — evidence of a new substance; milk mixed with water just gets thinner.

days.guide: Set up steel wool in three jars: dry, wet with water, wet with vinegar. Your child predicts which rusts most.

questions.q: Which do you predict will rust fastest?
questions.a: Steel wool with vinegar, then water; dry steel wool rusts very little.

days.guide: Make cabbage juice indicator; test 6 liquids and record colors. Adult chops and simmers red cabbage, then strains the purple juice. Your child adds a spoonful of juice to each liquid and records the color in a table, labeling acid or base.

questions.q: What color does cabbage juice turn in vinegar and in baking soda water?
questions.a: Pink/red in vinegar (acid); green/blue in baking soda water (base).

days.guide: Your child sorts 10 changes (melting ice, burning wood, rusting, dissolving sugar, baking a cake, cutting paper…) as new substance or not, with evidence. Check the rust jars.

questions.q: Is burning wood a chemical change? Is melting chocolate?
questions.a: Burning wood is chemical (new ash, gases, heat, light); melting chocolate is physical (same substance).

weeks.assessment_key: Sorting key: new substance — burning wood, rusting, baking a cake, baking soda + vinegar, milk + lemon curdling, fireworks; not new — melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper, boiling water, freezing juice. Observation tables: sign(s) of reaction recorded for each test.

weeks.prep: Plastic bottle, balloon, baking soda, vinegar, kitchen scale, cup, graph paper. Check the rust jars from last week. Write the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking mass is destroyed in a reaction. Particles rearrange; the gas escaped from the open cup.
Thinking the balloon gas weighs nothing. It's matter with mass.
Expecting the closed system to weigh exactly the same on every scale. A puffed balloon can push up slightly on the air, so expect tiny differences.

days.guide: Weigh vinegar and baking soda separately in an open cup, combine and weigh after bubbling stops. Record the change.

questions.q: Before: 150 g. After the open-cup reaction: 146 g. Where did 4 g go?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air.

days.guide: Repeat in a bottle sealed with a balloon holding the baking soda. Weigh before and after tipping it in.

questions.q: What do you expect the closed system to weigh after reacting?
questions.a: About the same as before — the gas is trapped in the balloon.

days.guide: Your child graphs both trials and explains the difference using gas particles escaping. Draw paired bars for before/after in each trial. Ask: 'Did the matter disappear or go somewhere?' to guide the gas explanation.

questions.q: Why does the open cup seem to lose weight?
questions.a: The gas produced (made of particles with mass) leaves the cup, so the scale no longer measures it.

days.guide: Examine the rust jars. Your child describes the evidence of a new substance and connects it to particles rearranging.

questions.q: What is the evidence of rust?
questions.a: Reddish-brown flaky material forms — a new substance made when iron combines with oxygen and water.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and the final CER. Give the test independently, then the CER on conservation in reactions using the open vs. closed data.

questions.q: Is mass conserved in a chemical reaction?
questions.a: Yes — the total mass of the substances before equals the total after, when nothing escapes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key (suggested): 1) mass is conserved when melting/freezing 2) 3 signs of a chemical reaction: gas, color change, new solid/temperature change 3) salt water is a solution 4) recovering salt by evaporation 5) open cup loses mass because gas escapes 6) closed system keeps mass constant 7) rust is a new substance 8) dissolving is not a chemical reaction. CER rubric: 4 = clear, accurate claim; specific evidence with numbers from the data; reasoning that links evidence to the science idea (particles, conservation, etc.); 3 = accurate claim and evidence, reasoning partial; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Plastic bottles (cut top off and invert as a funnel), sand, gravel, cotton balls, coffee filters, aquarium activated charcoal (rinse first), dirty water (soil, leaves, a drop of food coloring), play money for budgets. Safety: filtered water is never for drinking.
misconceptions: Thinking 'clear' means 'safe.' Filters do not remove all germs.
Changing many things at once. Test materials one at a time.
Confusing criteria and constraints. Criteria = what success looks like; constraints = limits.

days.guide: Read about communities without clean water. Your child writes the design problem, criteria (clearest water, enough volume) and constraints (materials, budget).

questions.q: Is 'cost under $10 of play money' a criterion or constraint?
questions.a: A constraint (a limit).

days.guide: Your child tests each material alone with the same amount of dirty water and rates clarity 1–5. Pour the same amount (e.g., 100 mL) through each material in a funnel. Your child compares to a clarity scale you make (1 = muddy, 5 = clear).

questions.q: Why test materials one at a time?
questions.a: To know which material does what, so the design uses each wisely.

days.guide: Your child sketches 3 filter designs with labeled layers and costs. Remind your child to label each layer and its cost. Ask why they put each layer in that order.

questions.q: Which layer usually goes at the top and why?
questions.a: Gravel, to catch large particles first so finer layers don't clog.

days.guide: Your child compares designs in a decision matrix and chooses one. Make a table with designs as rows and criteria (clarity, cost, speed) as columns, scoring 1–3. The highest total wins, unless a constraint rules it out.

questions.q: What is a decision matrix?
questions.a: A table scoring each design on the criteria and constraints to compare them fairly.

days.guide: Build the first prototype and write a prediction of how it will perform. Help cut and invert the bottle top. Your child writes a prediction with a reason before any water is poured.

questions.q: Predict a weakness.
questions.a: Example: sand may wash through cotton, making water cloudy.

weeks.assessment_key: Design notebook rubric: 4 = clear problem, criteria and constraints, 3 labeled sketches with costs, decision matrix with reasoning; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing a sketch or matrix; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Filter prototype, dirty water, measuring cup, timer, graph paper.
misconceptions: Changing more than one variable in version 2.
Believing a clear filter makes water drinkable. Germs remain; disinfection is needed.
Thinking failure is bad. Failure points guide improvement.

days.guide: Run the same volume (e.g., 200 mL) through the prototype. Your child records clarity (1–5), time and volume recovered.

questions.q: Why use the same amount of dirty water each time?
questions.a: It keeps the test fair so only the design affects the results.

days.guide: Your child identifies failure points and plans one change. Look at the data and the filter together. Your child names the one biggest problem and the single change to try.

questions.q: Water flows too slowly. What could you change?
questions.a: Use less fine material or a thinner sand layer.

days.guide: Build version 2, changing only one variable, and test under the same conditions. Use the same dirty water mix and volume as the first test. Your child records results in the same table.

questions.q: Why change only one variable?
questions.a: So you know that change caused any difference in results.

days.guide: Your child graphs both versions and discusses why filtered water still isn't safe. Graph clarity for each version side by side. Explain that germs are too small to be caught by sand and charcoal, so the water still needs boiling or treatment.

questions.q: Why isn't filtered water safe to drink?
questions.a: Bacteria, viruses and dissolved chemicals can pass through; water needs boiling or disinfection.

days.guide: Your child presents the final design and writes a reflection on how fair tests guided improvements. Your child presents in 3–5 minutes with the graph. Ask, 'What would version 3 change?'

questions.q: What made your tests fair?
questions.a: Same water amount, same dirty water mix, same timing, one change at a time.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = explains design, data for both versions graphed, identifies the one change and its effect, explains safety limitation; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = little data; 1 = incomplete. Graph: clarity/time per version with labels.

weeks.prep: Bean or radish seeds, potting soil (dry it in a sunny spot first), cups with drainage, kitchen scale, water, zip bags and paper towels. Read about Jan van Helmont's willow experiment (1600s).
misconceptions: Thinking plants 'eat' soil. Most plant mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air and water.
Thinking food for plants comes from fertilizer. Fertilizer supplies small amounts of nutrients, not most of the mass.
Weighing wet soil at the start and dry at the end. Use dry soil both times.

days.guide: Your child writes and draws initial ideas about where a giant tree's material comes from. Accept all ideas; this is a starting model.

questions.q: Where do you think a tree's mass comes from?
questions.a: Accept any initial idea; the scientific answer (to be learned) is mostly from carbon dioxide in the air plus water.

days.guide: Read about van Helmont's experiment: he planted a 5-pound willow in 200 pounds of dry soil and watered it for 5 years. The tree gained about 164 pounds; the soil lost only about 2 ounces.

questions.q: What did van Helmont's data show?
questions.a: The tree gained about 164 pounds but the soil lost only about 2 ounces, so the mass did not come from soil.

questions.q: What did he conclude, and was he fully right?
questions.a: He concluded it came from water; partly right — we now know most comes from carbon dioxide in the air, plus water.

days.guide: Weigh dry soil for each cup, plant seeds and record starting mass. Tare the scale with an empty cup, add dry soil and record the mass on the cup label. Plant 2–3 seeds per cup and water lightly.

questions.q: Why record the soil's starting mass?
questions.a: To compare at the end and see if soil mass decreased as the plant grew.

days.guide: Start seeds on wet paper towels in a bag with no soil. Fold a damp paper towel in a zip bag, place seeds inside and tape it to a window. Your child writes a prediction in the notebook.

questions.q: Predict: Can seeds sprout without soil?
questions.a: Yes — they sprout using stored food in the seed and water; with light, air and water they can keep growing for a while.

days.guide: Your child writes a preliminary claim about where plant mass comes from, citing van Helmont. Your child cites van Helmont's numbers (tree gained about 164 lb, soil lost about 2 oz). Accept 'water' or 'air' as hypotheses; the key is that it's not mainly soil.

questions.q: Write a preliminary claim.
questions.a: Plant mass does not come mainly from soil; it comes from something else, like water or air.

weeks.assessment_key: Initial model: any idea with a drawing. Preliminary claim rubric: 4 = claim that mass is not mainly from soil, citing van Helmont's numbers; 3 = claim with general evidence; 2 = claim only; 1 = none. Setup check: soil massed, seeds planted, data recorded.

weeks.prep: Spinach leaves, baking soda, water, needle-free syringe, a single-hole punch or straw, clear cups, lamp, clear nail polish, clear tape, magnifier or phone camera zoom. Leaf disk directions: dissolve 1/8 tsp baking soda in 300 mL water with a drop of dish soap; pull air out of disks with the syringe so they sink.
misconceptions: Thinking plants take in oxygen for photosynthesis. They take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
Thinking stomata are pores for water in only. Stomata let gases in and out and water vapor out.
Thinking plants don't need light to make food.

days.guide: Punch 10 spinach disks, remove air with the syringe so they sink in baking soda water, and place under a lamp. Count floating disks every minute.

questions.q: Why do the disks float after time under light?
questions.a: Photosynthesis produces oxygen gas inside the leaf, making the disks buoyant.

days.guide: Repeat the test in darkness and compare. Wrap a second cup in foil or place it in a closet, timing it the same as yesterday. Your child records both data sets in one table.

questions.q: What happens in the dark and what does it show?
questions.a: The disks stay down; without light, plants can't photosynthesize.

days.guide: Paint nail polish on the underside of a leaf, let dry, peel with tape, and look for stomata. Paint a small patch on the underside, let dry 10 minutes, then lift with tape and stick it on a dark paper or slide. Zoom with a magnifier or phone; stomata look like tiny lips or coffee beans.

questions.q: What are stomata?
questions.a: Tiny openings, mostly on the underside of leaves, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapor out.

days.guide: Measure plant heights in both setups and record growth. Measure from soil (or seed) to the top of the tallest leaf in centimeters. Record the date and compare with earlier measurements.

questions.q: Are the paper towel plants growing? Why might they stop?
questions.a: They grow at first from stored seed food and water; without soil nutrients they may slow over time.

days.guide: Your child draws a model: water entering roots, carbon dioxide entering leaves, light energy, sugar made, oxygen released. Take a quiz.

questions.q: What do plants make from air and water using light?
questions.a: Sugar (food), releasing oxygen.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) photosynthesis needs light, water, carbon dioxide 2) it produces sugar and oxygen 3) water enters through roots 4) carbon dioxide enters through stomata 5) leaf disks float because of oxygen 6) in the dark, disks don't float. Model diagram: arrows for water, CO2, light, sugar, O2 correctly placed.

weeks.prep: Food labels from 5 items, a thermometer, a jump rope, drawing supplies. Check if your child has any exercise restrictions.
misconceptions: Thinking food energy comes from the stomach. It originally comes from the sun captured by plants.
Thinking animals make their own energy from nothing.
Thinking calories are ingredients. Calories measure energy stored in food.

days.guide: List every breakfast food and trace each back to a plant and the sun with arrows (e.g., egg ← chicken ← corn ← sun). Model one chain. Your child does every breakfast food; check that every chain ends at a plant and then the sun.

questions.q: Trace milk back to the sun.
questions.a: Milk ← cow ← grass ← sun.

days.guide: Measure pulse and temperature at rest and after 2 minutes of jumping rope. Discuss how food energy powers motion and warmth.

questions.q: Why does your pulse rise after exercise?
questions.a: Muscles need more energy and oxygen, so the heart pumps faster; energy from food is used for movement and released as heat.

days.guide: Compare calories on 5 labels; explain calories measure stored energy originally from sunlight. Have your child put labels in order of calories per serving. Ask: 'Where did the plant get the energy stored in this food?'

questions.q: Where did the energy in a granola bar's calories originally come from?
questions.a: The sun — plants captured sunlight to make the oats, sugars and nuts.

days.guide: Your child creates an energy flow diagram: sun → grass → cow → human, labeling uses (growth, movement, body heat). Your child labels what each organism uses energy for. Point out that only some energy passes to the next level because much is used or lost as heat.

questions.q: Why do arrows point from the grass to the cow?
questions.a: Arrows show the direction energy and matter flow — from food to eater.

days.guide: Your child writes how the energy used to run a race was once energy from the sun. Encourage a step-by-step chain: sunlight → plant (photosynthesis) → food → my body → my muscles. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Model explanation.
questions.a: Sunlight was captured by plants and stored as sugar; I ate plants (or animals that ate plants) and my body used that stored energy to move my muscles in the race.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram and explanation rubric: 4 = complete chain from sun through producer and consumers, arrows in correct direction, uses of energy labeled, explanation names photosynthesis and stored energy; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = missing the sun or reversed arrows; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Plant cups from week 12, kitchen scale, graph paper. Spread soil to dry for a day before weighing. Write the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Expecting soil mass to drop by as much as plant mass increases.
Weighing plants wet with soil stuck on.
Ignoring air as a source of mass.

days.guide: Carefully remove plants, shake soil back into its cup, dry the soil, and weigh. Compare to the starting mass.

questions.q: What did you find about soil mass?
questions.a: It stayed about the same (only a tiny change).

days.guide: Weigh the plants (rinse soil off, pat dry). Record plant gain vs. soil change in a table.

questions.q: Plant gained 8 g; soil lost 0.2 g. What does this mean?
questions.a: Most of the plant's mass did not come from soil.

days.guide: Your child graphs soil mass change vs. plant mass gain for each cup.

questions.q: What pattern do you expect?
questions.a: Plant mass gains are much larger than soil losses.

days.guide: Your child writes an argument: claim, evidence from data and van Helmont, reasoning about air and water. Model the claim-evidence-reasoning format on a whiteboard. Evidence must include numbers from your cups.

questions.q: What is the reasoning?
questions.a: Plants use carbon dioxide from the air and water to make sugar through photosynthesis; that sugar builds the plant's body.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test; your child shares the argument aloud. Give the test independently. During the oral sharing, ask one 'why' question about the reasoning.

questions.q: Where does most of a plant's mass come from?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide from the air (with water).

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: 4 = claim (mass from air and water), evidence from own data with numbers and van Helmont, reasoning using photosynthesis; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = claim with weak evidence; 1 = incorrect claim. Unit 4 test key (suggested): 1) plant mass mainly from air and water 2) van Helmont's soil lost ~2 oz 3) photosynthesis needs light 4) stomata exchange gases 5) energy in food comes from the sun 6) calories measure stored energy.

weeks.prep: Index cards (make 20 kelp forest organism cards: giant kelp, phytoplankton, sea urchin, sea otter, sea star, abalone, rockfish, kelp crab, sea lion, great white shark, bacteria, worms, etc.), yarn, photos of a California kelp forest.
misconceptions: Drawing arrows from eaten to eater as 'eats.' Arrows point toward the eater to show energy flow.
Forgetting decomposers.
Thinking removing one species only affects its prey.

days.guide: Your child sorts the cards into producers (kelp, phytoplankton), consumers and decomposers (bacteria). Read each card's diet with your child before sorting. Ask: 'Does it make its own food from sunlight?' to decide producers.

questions.q: Is giant kelp a producer or consumer?
questions.a: A producer — it makes its own food through photosynthesis.

days.guide: Build 4 food chains with arrows showing energy and matter flow. Model one chain on the table with arrows. Remind your child that arrows point from food to eater.

questions.q: Write a kelp forest food chain.
questions.a: Kelp → sea urchin → sea otter (arrows point to the eater).

days.guide: Connect chains with yarn into a web. Identify organisms with many connections.

questions.q: What is a food web?
questions.a: Many connected food chains in an ecosystem.

days.guide: Remove otters and predict. Read about the real kelp forest decline.

questions.q: What happens without sea otters?
questions.a: Urchins increase and eat kelp, so kelp forests shrink ('urchin barrens').

days.guide: Your child draws a backyard food web and takes a vocabulary quiz. Brainstorm backyard organisms together (ants, robins, grass, worms). Check arrow direction and that decomposers are included.

questions.q: Name a backyard producer, consumer and decomposer.
questions.a: Grass/plants; insects, birds; worms, fungi, bacteria.

weeks.assessment_key: Vocabulary quiz key: producer (makes its own food), consumer (eats others), decomposer (breaks down dead matter), herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, food chain, food web, predator, prey. Backyard web: 8+ organisms, correct arrow direction, includes decomposers.

weeks.prep: Bread slices, zip bags, fruit scraps, clear bottle, soil, leaves, magnifier. Safety: keep mold bags sealed; dispose of them sealed (mold spores can trigger allergies).
misconceptions: Thinking mold comes from nowhere. Mold spores are in the air.
Thinking decomposers are pests. They return nutrients to soil.
Thinking dead things just disappear.

days.guide: Set up bread in sealed bags: dry, damp, fridge, warm. Label and date them. Your child predicts which molds first.

questions.q: Which do you predict will mold first?
questions.a: Damp bread in a warm place — mold grows best with moisture and warmth.

days.guide: Build a compost column with layers of soil, leaves and fruit scraps; your child draws day 1. Layer soil, leaves, fruit scraps, then soil again; mist lightly and poke air holes. Your child draws and labels day 1.

questions.q: Why add soil?
questions.a: Soil contains decomposers (bacteria, fungi, small organisms).

days.guide: Read about fungi, bacteria and worms; your child explains how each breaks down dead matter. Read short passages together. Your child makes a 3-column chart: decomposer, how it breaks matter down, what it returns to the soil.

questions.q: How do earthworms help decomposition?
questions.a: They eat dead plant matter and leave castings that enrich soil.

days.guide: Your child records and sketches changes with dates. Your child sketches each bag and the column with dates, noting color, fuzz and size changes. Compare with the predictions.

questions.q: What changes do you observe?
questions.a: Mold patches, color changes, softening fruit, possible smell.

days.guide: Your child adds decomposers to the food web with arrows to soil and air and explains the cycle. Use last week's web. Your child adds decomposers with arrows from dead organisms and waste to soil and air, then explains the cycle aloud.

questions.q: What happens to matter decomposers break down?
questions.a: It returns to the soil as nutrients and to the air as carbon dioxide; plants reuse it.

weeks.assessment_key: Observation log: dated sketches and notes for all bags and the column. Revised food web: decomposers connected to dead organisms with arrows to soil/air; explanation of matter cycling.

weeks.prep: Large jar with lid, gravel, soil, small plants or moss, optional pill bugs, spray bottle. Place the jar in bright, indirect light.
misconceptions: Thinking a closed jar runs out of water. Water cycles through evaporation and condensation.
Thinking plants only produce oxygen. They also use it.
Thinking nutrients come from outside.

days.guide: Build the terrarium: gravel, soil, plants, optional pill bugs. Your child diagrams its parts.

questions.q: Why put gravel at the bottom?
questions.a: For drainage so roots don't sit in water.

days.guide: Your child predicts how water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients will move. Ask about each substance: 'Where does it come from, where does it go?' Your child writes predictions with arrows.

questions.q: How will carbon dioxide move?
questions.a: Animals and decomposers release it; plants take it in for photosynthesis.

days.guide: Observe condensation and plant health. Look closely morning and afternoon. Your child records drops, fog and plant color in the notebook.

questions.q: Why does water form on the jar walls?
questions.a: Water evaporates from soil and leaves, then condenses on the cooler glass.

days.guide: Record final observations of mold bags and compost; compare to day 1. Your child compares final sketches with day 1 sketches and lists changes. Dispose of mold bags sealed in the trash.

questions.q: How did the compost change?
questions.a: Fruit and leaves broke down and shrank, becoming darker and more soil-like.

days.guide: Your child draws a matter-cycle model with arrows for water, gases and nutrients. Your child draws the jar with color-coded arrows: blue for water, green for gases, brown for nutrients. Check with the rubric.

questions.q: Where do nutrients come from in the sealed jar?
questions.a: Decomposers break down dead leaves and waste, returning nutrients to the soil.

weeks.assessment_key: Terrarium model rubric: 4 = arrows showing water (evaporation, condensation, uptake), gases (O2 and CO2 exchange), and nutrients (decomposition to soil to plants) labeled; 3 = two cycles; 2 = one; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Articles on quagga mussels or Argentine ants in California; graph paper; space for an 'Oh Deer' game (cards labeled food, water, shelter). Write the Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking invasive species are always bigger predators. Many are small and outcompete natives.
Thinking populations stay constant.
Reading predator-prey graphs as unrelated.

days.guide: Read about an invasive species; diagram how it disrupts the food web. Read together; your child draws the food web before and after the invasive species arrived. Ask what native species lost.

questions.q: How do quagga mussels harm lakes?
questions.a: They filter out plankton that native species need and clog pipes.

days.guide: Graph sample predator and prey data; describe the pattern. Provide sample data (e.g., rabbits and foxes over 10 years). Your child graphs both lines and describes how predator peaks follow prey peaks.

questions.q: What pattern do predator and prey populations show?
questions.a: They rise and fall in cycles; predator peaks follow prey peaks.

days.guide: Play 'Oh Deer' with family and record populations each round. Explain rules: 'deer' pick a needed resource, 'resource' players pick one; deer who match survive and reproduce. Your child records population each round and graphs it.

questions.q: What happens when resources are limited?
questions.a: The deer population drops; when it drops, resources recover and it rises again.

days.guide: Observe the terrarium; explain whether matter is cycling. Your child looks for condensation, new growth and decomposing leaves, writing a short claim about whether matter is cycling.

questions.q: What evidence shows matter cycling?
questions.a: Condensation, healthy plants, decomposing leaves.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test. Give the test without help, then review any missed vocabulary with the food web cards.

questions.q: Name the three roles in a food web.
questions.a: Producers, consumers, decomposers.

weeks.assessment_key: Population graph: both lines labeled, pattern described. Unit 5 test key (suggested): 1) producers make food 2) arrows show energy flow 3) removing otters increases urchins 4) decomposers return matter to soil 5) invasive species disrupt webs 6) predator-prey cycles 7) terrarium water cycle.

weeks.prep: Clipboard, colored pencils, NASA Earth images; NASA Space Place video on Earth's systems.
misconceptions: Thinking people aren't part of the biosphere.
Mixing up atmosphere and hydrosphere for clouds. Clouds are water (hydrosphere) in the atmosphere.
Thinking spheres work separately.

days.guide: Watch the video; your child makes a four-quadrant chart: geosphere (rocks, soil), hydrosphere (water, ice), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things). Watch together and pause after each sphere. Your child adds two examples to each quadrant.

questions.q: Name the four spheres with an example each.
questions.a: Geosphere: rocks; hydrosphere: ocean; atmosphere: air; biosphere: trees.

days.guide: Survey a yard or park; list 10 things and label each sphere. Walk the yard with a clipboard. Your child writes 10 observations and labels each sphere.

questions.q: Which sphere is a puddle? A bird?
questions.a: Hydrosphere; biosphere.

days.guide: Identify 5 interactions and draw arrows. Model one interaction with an arrow and label. Your child adds 5 interactions from the survey.

questions.q: Example interaction.
questions.a: Rain (atmosphere/hydrosphere) soaks soil (geosphere).

days.guide: Examine hurricane and wildfire images; identify interacting spheres. View the images together. Ask which spheres are causing changes and which are being changed.

questions.q: Which spheres interact in a hurricane?
questions.a: Warm ocean water (hydrosphere) evaporates into the atmosphere, fueling storms that affect land and living things.

days.guide: Give the spheres quiz; your child explains one interaction in a paragraph. Give the quiz and have your child write a paragraph explaining one interaction with cause and effect.

questions.q: How do plant roots affect rocks?
questions.a: Roots (biosphere) grow into cracks and break rocks (geosphere).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: geosphere = rock/soil; hydrosphere = water; atmosphere = air; biosphere = life. Interaction chart: 5 arrows labeled. Paragraph: names 2 spheres and explains cause and effect.

weeks.prep: Baking pan, sand and soil, watering can, rocks, jar with lid, sugar cubes, hair dryer. Work outside or on a tray.
misconceptions: Mixing up weathering and erosion. Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves pieces.
Thinking deposition is erosion. Deposition is where sediment is dropped.
Thinking plants have no effect on erosion.

days.guide: Shake sugar cubes in a jar with water for 3 minutes and observe. Shake for 3 full minutes and observe the sugar cubes or rocks. Ask what real-world process this models (rocks tumbling in a river).

questions.q: What happened to the cubes and what does it model?
questions.a: Corners broke and rounded — physical weathering, like rocks in a river.

days.guide: Build a sloped pan and pour water slowly; sketch the channel and delta. Prop the pan on a book; pour slowly from one end. Your child sketches where sand was removed and where it collected.

questions.q: Where is sand deposited?
questions.a: At the bottom where water slows, forming a delta.

days.guide: Repeat with a steeper slope and with grass clumps; compare. Change only one thing each time (slope, then plants). Your child compares sketches and states which caused more erosion.

questions.q: How did a steeper slope and plants change erosion?
questions.a: Steeper = more erosion; plants = less erosion because roots hold soil.

days.guide: Blow a hair dryer on dry sand vs. wet sand.

questions.q: Which erodes more?
questions.a: Dry sand; water holds grains together.

days.guide: Your child writes about sphere interactions in the models and a CA example. Your child connects at least two models to spheres and to a California landform (Yosemite or coastal cliffs).

questions.q: How was Yosemite Valley shaped?
questions.a: Glaciers (hydrosphere) carved the valley in granite (geosphere), and rivers continue to erode it.

weeks.assessment_key: Written explanation rubric: 4 = defines weathering, erosion, deposition, explains model results and connects to a CA example with spheres; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = definitions only; 1 = incomplete. Sketches: channel and delta labeled.

weeks.prep: Jar, hot water (adult), ice in a plate on top, food coloring, clear container, thermometer, weather log sheet. Look up average temperatures for San Francisco and Sacramento.
misconceptions: Thinking clouds are water vapor. Clouds are tiny liquid droplets.
Thinking the ocean has no effect on land temperatures.
Mixing up weather and climate.

days.guide: Pour hot water in a jar, place a plate of ice on top; observe a cloud. Adult pours hot water; place ice on a plate on top. Optional: light a match briefly and drop it in for smoke particles (adult only) to help droplets form.

questions.q: Why does a cloud form?
questions.a: Warm water vapor rises, cools near the ice and condenses into tiny droplets.

days.guide: Model currents with colored hot and cold water in a clear container. Fill a clear container with room-temperature water. Gently add blue ice water and red hot water at opposite ends and observe.

questions.q: What does cold water do?
questions.a: Sinks because it is denser; warm water rises.

days.guide: Your child records temperature, clouds and precipitation daily. Record at the same time each day in a log. Discuss changes at the end of the week.

questions.q: Weather vs. climate?
questions.a: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the long-term average.

days.guide: Compare SF and Sacramento temperatures; explain ocean effects. Look up average monthly highs. Your child graphs both cities and explains the ocean's moderating effect.

questions.q: Why are SF summers cooler than Sacramento's?
questions.a: The cool Pacific Ocean and fog moderate SF; inland Sacramento heats up (July highs about 90s°F vs. upper 60s°F in SF).

days.guide: Your child draws a model of a rainstorm with spheres interacting. Your child draws the storm with arrows labeled with sphere names and processes.

questions.q: Describe sphere interactions in a rainstorm.
questions.a: Ocean water evaporates into the atmosphere, falls as rain on land, and plants and animals use it.

weeks.assessment_key: Model rubric: 4 = three spheres, arrows for evaporation, condensation, precipitation, uptake by living things; 3 = two spheres; 2 = one; 1 = incomplete. Weather log: 5 days complete.

weeks.prep: Articles on a California wildfire followed by mudslides (e.g., the 2017 Thomas Fire and 2018 Montecito debris flows), poster board. Note: real disasters involved loss of life — preview for sensitive children. Write the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking events have one cause.
Forgetting humans are in the biosphere.
Thinking burned land absorbs more water. Burned soil can repel water, increasing runoff.

days.guide: Read the case study; list spheres involved. Read the article aloud; preview for sensitive details. Your child lists each sphere with an example from the event.

questions.q: Which spheres were involved?
questions.a: Biosphere (vegetation burned), atmosphere (smoke, rain), geosphere (soil, mud), hydrosphere (rain, runoff).

days.guide: Build a cause-effect chain. Model the first link. Your child builds a chain on paper strips linking fire to mudslides.

questions.q: Why did mudslides follow the fire?
questions.a: Fire removed plants whose roots held soil; heavy rain washed loose soil and debris downhill.

days.guide: Create a poster model with labeled arrows. Your child sketches the hillside before and after, with arrows labeled for each interaction.

questions.q: How did the atmosphere affect the fire?
questions.a: Dry, hot winds (Santa Anas) spread the fire.

days.guide: Present the model; answer questions on humans in the biosphere. Your child presents for 2–3 minutes. Ask how people changed the area and how they might reduce future risk.

questions.q: How are humans part of this?
questions.a: Humans live in the area, can start fires, fight fires and rebuild.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Give the test independently and review missed items with the poster.

questions.q: Name an interaction between biosphere and geosphere.
questions.a: Roots hold soil in place.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = all four spheres with labeled interactions and a clear cause-effect chain; 3 = three spheres; 2 = two; 1 = incomplete. Unit 6 test key (suggested): four spheres defined; weathering vs erosion; deposition; plants reduce erosion; clouds from condensation; ocean moderates climate.

weeks.prep: 1 L water bottle, measuring cups/spoons, eyedropper, graph paper, USGS water distribution data (Water Science School).
misconceptions: Thinking most water is fresh. About 97% is salt water.
Thinking most fresh water is in lakes and rivers. Most is ice and groundwater.
Thinking water is unlimited because the water cycle recycles it.

days.guide: Pour 970 mL into a container for ocean (97%). Divide the remaining 30 mL: about 20 mL ice, about 9 mL groundwater, and about 1 mL (a few drops) surface water.

questions.q: Of Earth's water, about what percent is salt water?
questions.a: About 97%.

days.guide: Read USGS data; record percentages. Read the USGS page together. Your child records percentages in a table.

questions.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
questions.a: In ice caps and glaciers (about 69%), then groundwater (about 30%).

days.guide: Make circle and bar graphs. Help divide a circle into 97% and 3%. Your child makes a second graph of fresh water reservoirs.

questions.q: What portion of fresh water is in lakes and rivers?
questions.a: Around 1% or less of fresh water.

days.guide: Answer data questions. Your child answers questions using the graphs, citing numbers.

questions.q: What fraction of fresh water is easily available?
questions.a: Only a tiny fraction (about 1%) is in lakes, rivers and soil.

days.guide: Your child writes why fresh water is limited, using graphs. Your child writes a paragraph with at least two percentages as evidence.

questions.q: Why is fresh water limited?
questions.a: Only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is frozen or underground.

weeks.assessment_key: Graphs: accurate proportions, labels. Explanation rubric: 4 = uses percentages from graphs and explains that easily available fresh water is tiny; 3 = mostly; 2 = general; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Map of California water systems (e.g., DWR map of State Water Project, Central Valley Project, LA Aqueduct), zip bag, marker, tape, clear cup, gravel, sand, clay. Write the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Thinking groundwater is an underground lake. It fills spaces between rock and sand.
Thinking all CA water comes from local rain.
Ignoring snowpack as storage.

days.guide: Draw the water cycle on a zip bag with a little water; tape it to a sunny window. Draw sun, clouds, mountains and ocean on the bag with marker; add 1/4 cup water and tape it to a sunny window. Check after a few hours.

questions.q: What happens in the bag?
questions.a: Water evaporates, condenses on the top and drips down, like rain.

days.guide: Read about Sierra Nevada snowpack; trace how it reaches cities via rivers and aqueducts. Read about the snowpack and look at a map of aqueducts. Your child traces the path from mountains to your city.

questions.q: Why is the snowpack important?
questions.a: It stores water in winter and melts slowly in spring and summer, supplying roughly a third of California's water.

days.guide: Build an aquifer model and pour 'rain.' Layer gravel, sand and clay in a clear cup. Pour water slowly and watch where it collects.

questions.q: Where does the water go?
questions.a: Through sand and gravel; clay slows it, forming a groundwater layer.

days.guide: Estimate household water use in one day. Use a stopwatch and measuring cup to estimate flow rates. Your child totals daily household use.

questions.q: A 10-minute shower at 2 gallons per minute uses?
questions.a: 20 gallons.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. Give the test without help, then review graph-reading questions.

questions.q: Name a CA water source.
questions.a: Sierra Nevada snowpack/rivers, groundwater, Colorado River.

weeks.assessment_key: Water audit: estimates for faucets, shower, toilet, total. Unit 7 test key (suggested): 97% salt water; most fresh water frozen; groundwater; snowpack; aqueducts; graph reading items correct.

weeks.prep: NASA Climate Kids and EPA kids pages; index cards and petroleum jelly; gloves for trash audit; scale.
misconceptions: Thinking renewable resources can't be overused.
Thinking recycling solves all waste.
Thinking air pollution is only from factories.

days.guide: Your child sorts 15 resources as renewable or nonrenewable. Use resource cards. Your child sorts and explains how each is used at home.

questions.q: Is natural gas renewable?
questions.a: No — it's nonrenewable (fossil fuel).

questions.q: Is solar energy renewable?
questions.a: Yes.

days.guide: Coat cards with petroleum jelly; place indoors and outdoors. Place one card indoors and one outdoors for the week. Your child predicts which will collect more.

questions.q: What will the cards collect?
questions.a: Dust, pollen, soot — particulates in the air.

days.guide: Weigh and sort one day of trash. Wear gloves; weigh each category on a scale. Your child records in a table and graphs.

questions.q: Which category is largest?
questions.a: Varies; discuss how to reduce it.

days.guide: Read two impact articles; take notes. Read together. Your child notes the problem, cause and a possible solution for each.

questions.q: How does plastic harm the ocean?
questions.a: Animals eat it or get tangled; it breaks into microplastics.

days.guide: Examine cards; write a summary of human impacts on two spheres. Examine cards with a magnifier. Your child writes a summary of human impacts on two spheres.

questions.q: Name one human impact on the atmosphere.
questions.a: Burning fossil fuels releases pollution and carbon dioxide.

weeks.assessment_key: Trash audit: categories weighed. Summary rubric: 4 = two spheres, specific impacts with evidence; 3 = mostly; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Articles on Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, water-wise landscaping, California condor recovery; city website; note sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking conservation is only government work.
Using one source only.
Copying facts without credit.

days.guide: Read two case studies; record problem, science, results. Read the case studies together. Your child fills a chart with problem, science used, result.

questions.q: How was the condor saved?
questions.a: By 1987 all 27 remaining wild condors were captured for breeding; captive-bred birds were released and now over 500 exist.

days.guide: Find city recycling, stormwater and conservation practices. Browse the city website together. Your child writes three facts about local programs.

questions.q: What does storm drain water flow into?
questions.a: Usually directly to creeks and the ocean without treatment.

days.guide: Interview a family member about conservation. Your child prepares 3–5 questions and records answers.

questions.q: Example question.
questions.a: What do you do to save water at home?

days.guide: Combine notes from 3 sources into a fact sheet. Your child groups facts by topic and credits each source.

questions.q: How do you combine sources?
questions.a: Group facts by topic and credit each source.

days.guide: Share the fact sheet; take a quiz. Your child shares the fact sheet aloud; give the quiz.

questions.q: Name 2 conservation strategies.
questions.a: Drip irrigation, recycling, protected areas.

weeks.assessment_key: Fact sheet rubric: 4 = 3 sources credited, accurate facts, organized; 3 = 2 sources; 2 = 1 source; 1 = incomplete. Quiz key: reduce, reuse, recycle; water-wise plants; protected marine areas; species recovery.

weeks.prep: Recycled materials, tape, scissors, water, vegetable oil, cotton, feathers, sponge. Write the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Changing several variables.
Thinking a prototype must work first try.
Ignoring trade-offs.

days.guide: Choose a problem; define criteria and constraints. Discuss both problems; your child chooses one. They write two criteria and two constraints.

questions.q: Criteria for oil spill cleanup?
questions.a: Removes the most oil, quickly.

days.guide: Sketch two solutions; compare trade-offs. Your child sketches two designs and lists one pro and one con of each.

questions.q: What is a trade-off?
questions.a: Giving up one benefit to gain another.

days.guide: Build and test a prototype. Your child builds and tests, recording data (e.g., how much oil remains).

questions.q: Which material absorbs oil best?
questions.a: Usually cotton or sponge.

days.guide: Identify a failure point; change one variable; retest. Your child identifies the main failure and changes one thing.

questions.q: Why retest?
questions.a: To see if the change improved results.

days.guide: Present the solution; take the Unit 8 test. Your child presents; give the test.

questions.q: How is a real oil spill cleaned?
questions.a: Booms contain oil; skimmers and absorbents remove it.

weeks.assessment_key: Engineering notebook rubric: problem, sketches, data, improvement. Unit 8 test key (suggested): renewable vs. nonrenewable; human impacts; conservation strategies; engineering design steps.

weeks.prep: String, washer (plumb line), balls of different masses, globe, small figurines; PhET 'Gravity and Orbits.'
misconceptions: Thinking heavier objects fall faster. Without air resistance, they fall at the same rate.
Thinking people in Australia would fall off. 'Down' is toward Earth's center everywhere.
Thinking gravity only works on Earth.

days.guide: Drop balls of different masses from the same height; record which lands first. Drop pairs from the same height at the same moment. Your child records which lands first over 3 trials.

questions.q: Which lands first?
questions.a: They land at about the same time.

days.guide: Make a plumb line and test it in different places. Tie a washer to string; hold it still in several locations. Your child notes the direction each time.

questions.q: Does the plumb line always point the same direction?
questions.a: Yes — straight down toward Earth's center.

days.guide: Place figurines around a globe and draw 'down' arrows. Tape figurines on the globe. Your child draws 'down' arrows pointing to the center.

questions.q: Which way is down in Australia?
questions.a: Toward Earth's center.

days.guide: Explore the simulation; record how gravity affects motion. Explore the simulation together. Your child records what happens when gravity is turned off.

questions.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit?
questions.a: Earth's gravity pulls it.

days.guide: Your child writes an argument that gravity on Earth is directed toward its center. Your child writes claim, evidence from three investigations, and reasoning.

questions.q: Give a piece of evidence.
questions.a: Plumb lines point straight down everywhere; people everywhere stand upright.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: 4 = claim, evidence from plumb line, drop test and globe model, reasoning; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = claim only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Two identical flashlights, measuring tape, dark room, optional light meter app; NASA Space Place 'What is a Star?'
misconceptions: Thinking the sun is a different kind of object than stars. It's a medium-sized star.
Thinking brighter means bigger.
Thinking distance doesn't affect brightness.

days.guide: Read 'What is a Star?'; compare the sun to other stars. Read together; your child compares the sun to other stars in a chart (size, temperature, distance).

questions.q: Is the sun a star?
questions.a: Yes — a medium-sized star.

days.guide: Compare flashlights at 1 m, 3 m, 6 m. In a dark room, compare flashlights at different distances. Your child records observations.

questions.q: Which looks brightest?
questions.a: The closest one.

days.guide: Measure brightness with a light meter or paper layers; graph. Use a light meter app or count paper layers needed to block light. Your child graphs brightness vs. distance.

questions.q: What pattern do you see?
questions.a: Brightness decreases as distance increases.

days.guide: Compare distances of the sun, Sirius and Betelgeuse with a scale model. Use a hallway or sidewalk scale. Your child marks the sun, Sirius and Betelgeuse distances.

questions.q: How far is Sirius?
questions.a: About 8.6 light-years; the sun is about 8 light-minutes away.

days.guide: Your child writes a CER on why the sun looks brighter. Your child writes the CER using the flashlight data as evidence.

questions.q: Claim.
questions.a: The sun looks brighter because it is much closer than other stars.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = clear, accurate claim; specific evidence with numbers from the data; reasoning that links evidence to the science idea (particles, conservation, etc.); 3 = accurate claim and evidence, reasoning partial; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only or inaccurate. Graph: distance vs brightness with labeled axes.

weeks.prep: Toilet paper roll, measuring tape, markers, balls of different sizes. Write the Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking planets are close together.
Thinking orbits need no force.
Thinking all stars are at the same distance.

days.guide: Build a toilet-paper model: Mercury 1, Venus 1.8, Earth 2.5, Mars 3.8, Jupiter 13, Saturn 24, Uranus 48, Neptune 75 sheets from the sun. Unroll toilet paper along a hallway; mark planets with sticky notes. Ask what surprised them.

questions.q: What do you notice about outer planets?
questions.a: They are much farther apart.

days.guide: Compare sizes with balls and seeds. Use balls and seeds to compare sizes. Discuss why distance and size models are hard to combine.

questions.q: How many Earths fit across the sun?
questions.a: About 109.

days.guide: Swing a ball on a string; discuss gravity and orbits. Swing a ball on a string in a safe area. Ask what happens when you let go.

questions.q: What happens if the string is cut?
questions.a: The ball flies off in a straight line.

days.guide: Analyze a star brightness table. Your child reads a brightness and distance table and identifies a pattern.

questions.q: What pattern?
questions.a: Closer stars generally appear brighter, but bigger or hotter stars can be bright far away.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test. Give the test without help.

questions.q: What force keeps planets in orbit?
questions.a: Gravity.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key (suggested): gravity pulls toward Earth's center; objects fall at same rate; sun is a star; brightness depends on distance; gravity keeps planets in orbit. Reflection: scale model insight.

weeks.prep: Stick or pencil in clay, chalk, measuring tape, compass, flashlight, globe, toothpick. Pick a sunny day.
misconceptions: Thinking the sun moves around Earth.
Thinking shadows are always the same length.
Thinking noon shadows point south. In California they point north.

days.guide: Set up a shadow stick; mark and measure the shadow hourly from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

questions.q: When is the shadow shortest?
questions.a: Near midday (solar noon), when the sun is highest.

days.guide: Graph shadow length vs. time.

questions.q: What pattern?
questions.a: Long in the morning, shortest at midday, long again in the afternoon.

days.guide: Record shadow direction with a compass. Use a compass to label N, S, E, W. Your child records direction each hour.

questions.q: Why does the shadow move?
questions.a: Earth rotates, so the sun's position in the sky changes; shadows move from west (morning) toward east (afternoon).

days.guide: Model with a flashlight, globe and toothpick on California. Darken the room; shine a flashlight on the globe. Rotate it and watch the toothpick's shadow.

questions.q: What causes day and night?
questions.a: Earth's rotation.

days.guide: Build a sundial; explain how rotation causes shadow patterns. Your child builds a paper sundial and writes an explanation.

questions.q: How does a sundial tell time?
questions.a: The shadow moves predictably as Earth rotates.

weeks.assessment_key: Graph: time vs length, U-shaped. Explanation rubric: 4 = Earth's rotation, sun's apparent motion, length and direction changes; 3 = mostly; 2 = partial; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Sunrise/sunset data table for your city, graph paper, globe, lamp.
misconceptions: Thinking seasons are caused by distance from the sun. They're caused by Earth's tilt.
Thinking day length is the same everywhere.
Thinking the longest day is in July.

days.guide: Collect sunrise and sunset times for the first of each month; calculate daylight hours. Use an almanac or website for sunrise/sunset times. Your child calculates daylight hours.

questions.q: Sunrise 6:00 a.m., sunset 8:00 p.m. — daylight hours?
questions.a: 14 hours.

days.guide: Graph daylight across the year; find longest and shortest. Your child graphs months on the x-axis and hours on the y-axis.

questions.q: When are the longest and shortest days?
questions.a: Around June 21 and December 21.

days.guide: Model with a lamp and tilted globe. Tilt the globe about 23.5° and orbit the lamp. Your child observes the Northern Hemisphere in summer and winter.

questions.q: Why are summer days longer?
questions.a: Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the sun, so more of its daily path is in sunlight.

days.guide: Compare Los Angeles and Anchorage. Your child compares graphs for both cities and describes differences.

questions.q: How does Anchorage differ?
questions.a: Much longer summer days (about 19 hours) and shorter winter days (about 5.5 hours).

days.guide: Answer data questions; take a quiz. Give the data-analysis questions and quiz.

questions.q: What causes seasons?
questions.a: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the sun.

weeks.assessment_key: Day length graph: monthly points, labeled. Quiz key: tilt causes seasons; longest ~June 21; shortest ~Dec 21; higher latitudes have bigger changes.

weeks.prep: Star chart or free planetarium app, red flashlight, lamp, constellation pictures. Check the weather for a clear night; supervise outdoor observation.
misconceptions: Thinking stars move on their own each night. Their apparent motion is due to Earth's rotation.
Thinking the same stars are visible all year.
Thinking constellations are close together in space.

days.guide: Go outside after dark; sketch 2 constellations and positions. Choose a clear night; let eyes adjust 10–15 minutes. Your child sketches constellations with landmarks for position.

questions.q: Why use a red flashlight?
questions.a: It preserves night vision.

days.guide: Walk around a lamp with constellations on the walls. Tape constellation pictures on four walls. Your child walks around the lamp, noting which pictures face the 'night' side.

questions.q: Why do we see different stars in different seasons?
questions.a: As Earth orbits the sun, the night side faces different directions in space.

days.guide: Record when Orion, Scorpius and the Big Dipper are visible at 9 p.m. Use a planetarium app and set the time to 9 p.m. for different months. Your child records in a table.

questions.q: When is Orion visible in the evening?
questions.a: Winter (December–March).

days.guide: Observe the sky again 2 hours later. Observe again 2 hours later. Your child notes the change in position.

questions.q: How did constellations move?
questions.a: East to west, because Earth rotates.

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 assessment. Give the test without help.

questions.q: When is Scorpius visible?
questions.a: Summer evenings.

weeks.assessment_key: Observation sketches: two constellations with positions and times. Unit 10 test key: shadow patterns; day length; tilt; seasonal stars; Earth's rotation.

weeks.prep: Materials for the chosen investigation; science notebook.
misconceptions: Testable questions must be measurable.
Too many variables.
Too few trials.

days.guide: Your child chooses a testable question. Brainstorm questions together. Your child picks one that is measurable.

questions.q: Is 'Do plants like music?' testable?
questions.a: Rewrite to: 'Does music affect bean plant height in 2 weeks?'

days.guide: Write a hypothesis, variables and procedure. Your child writes the hypothesis, variables, controls and steps.

questions.q: Name the independent and dependent variables.
questions.a: Independent = what you change; dependent = what you measure.

days.guide: Run at least 3 trials and record data. Your child runs at least 3 trials and records data.

questions.q: Why 3 trials?
questions.a: To make results reliable.

days.guide: Finish trials; organize data. Your child finishes trials and organizes data in a table with averages.

questions.q: How to organize data?
questions.a: A table with trials and averages.

days.guide: Make a graph; check accuracy with a parent. Your child graphs results; check scales and labels together.

questions.q: Which graph fits?
questions.a: Bar graph for categories; line graph for change over time.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan rubric: testable question, hypothesis, variables, procedure, 3 trials, data table.

weeks.prep: Tri-fold board or slides, graphs, photos.
misconceptions: Hypothesis 'wrong' means failure.
Conclusions without data.
Ignoring sources of error.

days.guide: Analyze data; decide if hypothesis was supported. Your child describes patterns in the data and decides if the hypothesis was supported.

questions.q: What if the data didn't support the hypothesis?
questions.a: That is still a valid result; explain what you learned.

days.guide: Write a conclusion with error sources and a new question. Your child writes a conclusion, error sources and a new question.

questions.q: Example error source.
questions.a: Inconsistent measuring.

days.guide: Create a board or slideshow. Your child creates the display with all sections.

questions.q: What sections?
questions.a: Question, hypothesis, procedure, data, graph, conclusion.

days.guide: Present to family or a co-op science fair. Your child presents and answers questions.

questions.q: How to answer a question you don't know?
questions.a: Say so and suggest how to find out.

days.guide: Your child reviews the notebook and writes about the three most important ideas. Your child reviews the notebook and writes about three big ideas.

questions.q: Example big idea.
questions.a: Matter is made of particles and is conserved.

weeks.assessment_key: Science fair rubric (4 levels): question and hypothesis; controlled procedure; data and graph; conclusion with error; presentation. Reflection: 3 big ideas explained.
